evidence_set: Two groups of people who all used several drugs, recruited at private parties or a nightclub and aged 18 to 29: 20 who had taken ketamine that evening within 30 minutes before testing, and 19 who had little or no previous ketamine use and had not taken it that evening. Both groups were tested on the night (day 0) in a small quiet room away from the music and again 3 days later (day 3) in their homes, with the same 25–35-minute battery in the same order; 7 more people tested once were not retested and 2 were discarded for taking drugs on the day of the second session. Story (prose) recall was scored in idea units, maximum 21, and the speed of comprehension test asked people to judge as many of 100 sentences as they could in 2 minutes. The self-ratings were an adapted dissociative states scale, a state schizotypal symptom questionnaire built for the study, a mood scale, 14 symptom ratings anchored at no symptom and severe symptom, and an anxiety and depression questionnaire rated for the last two days; no measure asked why people took ketamine or whether they enjoyed it.

Category fluency was lower in the ketamine group on both days (group F(1,37) = 21.1; day 3 14.85 (3.08) against 19.68 (4.58)) without a group × day interaction, and its day-3 score did not differ significantly from the comparison group's first-night score. Sentences correctly judged were lower on both days (day 3 63.30 (16.04) against 79.11 (19.94); interaction F(1,37) = 28.9), and the ketamine group's day-3 score is reported as significantly below the comparison group's first-night score (p<0.009). Editors' calculation from Table 1 (independent t-test, pooled SD): this check gives t(37) = 2.11, p ≈ 0.04 for sentence judging, almost the same as for category fluency (t(37) = 2.07, p ≈ 0.046), which the paper reports as not significant (card sc_curran_2000, reporting issues).

On the night both groups scored similarly low on story recall and category fluency: immediate story recall 4.67 (2.59) and 5.00 (3.66), category fluency 11.83 (4.32) and 12.58 (6.54), although letter fluency was already lower in the more frequent group (10.39 (6.01) against 17.42 (7.22)); dissociation was very high (34.83 (21.60) and 39.26 (25.32)) and so were state schizotypal scores (54.11 (30.22) and 53.58 (28.39)). Three days later dissociation (4.56 (6.35) and 3.47 (5.56)) and schizotypal scores (25.28 (19.80) and 28.95 (21.37)) had fallen in both groups (day effects F(1,35) = 78.1 and 48.2) with no group differences; serial sevens and cancellation improved in both groups (F(1,35) = 14.10 and 18.1) without group differences; all participants rated more sedation and both groups more anxiety on the night than on day 3 (F(1,35) = 41.8 and 9.33); and bodily numbness fell from 54.89 and 60.21 to 8.00 and 3.68.

Three days later the group using ketamine twice a month or less recalled 9.16 (3.86) ideas immediately and 8.05 (4.05) after a delay, against 4.56 (1.96) and 4.39 (1.57) in the group using it more often, whose immediate recall was no higher than on the night (4.67 (2.59)), although its delayed recall rose from 3.11 (2.28) (immediate recall group × day F(1,35) = 13.5; delayed F(1,35) = 6.7, printed p<0.01); category fluency was 18.95 (4.45) against 14.06 (3.83) (interaction F(1,35) = 4.18, p<0.05); letter fluency was lower in the more frequent group on both days (10.39 against 17.42, then 14.00 against 22.10). Highest qualification, more frequent against less frequent group: degree 0 against 4, GCSE 12 against 5; all participants reported no ketamine between the two sessions; the authors say baseline differences between the groups cannot be ruled out. Editors' calculation: F(1,35) = 6.7 corresponds to p ≈ 0.014.

evidence_set: A second narrative review, written for a UK scientific committee, describes ketamine as a non-competitive antagonist at the NMDA receptor, one of three glutamate receptors, central to learning and memory; it adds that ketamine blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, may strengthen GABA inhibition, induces dopamine release and acts as a weak opioid agonist, and that the two mirror-image forms differ in their affinity at the NMDA receptor while having similar pharmacokinetic profiles. Several of these statements carry no reference, and where the review cites imaging studies for striatal dopamine release two of the three papers are, by their titles, not dopamine-binding studies.
